texts: Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instances
notes: AWS Systems Manager is a management service that helps a user:
Collect software inventory
Apply OS patches
Create system images
Configure Windows and Linux operating systems

AWS Systems Manager is designed to be highly automation-focused, which enables the configuration and management of systems running on-premises or in AWS. AWS Systems Manager lets a user select the instances they want to manage and define the management tasks they want to perform.
AWS Systems Manager offers many features and benefits that systems operations specialists should find useful.

For example, the Run Command feature allows you to remotely run scripts and programs, while State Manager ensures that your EC2 instances are bootstrapped with specific software at startup. You can use Inventory Manager to collect and query information about the configuration and inventory of your EC2 instances and the software installed on them. And with Maintenance Window, you can define a recurring window of time to run administrative and maintenance tasks across your instances.
In this next section, there is an instructor demo, followed by an explanation of some of the key AWS Systems Manager features and benefits.
After the demo, the next few slides take a closer look at each of the Systems Manager features that are listed here.

texts: Demo: Features of AWS Systems Manager

texts: Safely automate common and repetitive IT operations and management tasks across AWS resources.
notes: The Automation feature in Systems Manager can define common IT tasks as a collection of steps in an AWS Systems Manager document (SSM document). The Automation feature can then run all document steps on an entire collection of AWS resources. For example, you could define an automation to remediate unreachable instances, create golden Amazon Machine Images (AMI) (AMIs), or patch instances. Custom automations can also be authored in JavaScript Object Notation (JSON). Amazon CloudWatch Events can also be configured to trigger Systems Manager automations.
A suggested approach to developing and testing a Systems Manager automation is to:
Create an automation document—or use an existing automation template—that includes sequential steps and parameters that Systems Manager runs.
Run the automation using Systems Manager, which will do things such as:
Launch an instance
Take a snapshot
Tag instances
Delete old images
Terminate an instance

Monitor the automation workflow (for example, using the AWS Management Console). After the automation finishes, confirm that the expected results were achieved. For example, you could launch a test instance from an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) that was updated by a Systems Manager automation to verify that it has the expected characteristics.

texts: Example command types provided by Amazon
notes: The Systems Manager Run Command provides a simple way to run predefined commands against EC2 instances. A command that is run by Run Command reduces management overhead because a user can manage instances without setting up bastion hosts or managing Secure Shell (SSH) keys and certificates.

Through integration with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), you can apply granular permissions to control the actions that users can perform on instances. All actions taken with Systems Manager can also be recorded by AWS CloudTrail, which allows a user to audit changes throughout their environment.

texts: Securely connect to instances without opening inbound ports, using bastion hosts, or maintaining SSH keys.
notes: The Session Manager feature in AWS Systems Manager lets a user manage their EC2 instances through an interactive browser-based shell that is accessible in the AWS Management Console.
Session Manager provides secure and auditable instance management without the need to open inbound ports in the security groups, maintain bastion host instances in EC2 subnets, or manage SSH keys.

Session Manager also makes it straightforward to comply with corporate policies that require controlled access to instances, strict security practices, and auditable logs that contain instance access details. A user can gain these benefits while still providing access to EC2 instances for end users.

texts: Deploy operating system and software patches automatically across large groups of Amazon EC2 or on-premises instances
notes: There are several challenges associated with patching servers and instances, including:
The time that it takes to patch multiple EC2 instances or on-premises machines
The repetitive nature of the task
How errors can result in downtime
Compliance issues
To use the Systems Manager Patch Manager to automate patching:
Create a patch baseline, which contains rules that automatically approve or reject patches.
Define a maintenance window, and group instances together for patching.
Apply patches in the maintenance window, and reboot every instance in the patch group.
Review the results and the details of patch compliance.

texts: Maintain consistent configuration of Amazon EC2 or on-premises instances
notes: AWS Systems Manager State Manager is a secure and scalable configuration management service that automates the process of keeping your EC2 and hybrid infrastructure in a state that you define.

You can install software when you create EC2 instances, download and update agents, configure network settings, join a Windows domain, patch instances with software updates, and run scripts on Linux and Windows managed instances.
Here’s how State Manager works:

First, create the AWS Systems Manager (SSM) document or identify an existing one that defines the actions that Systems Manager will perform on your managed instances. Documents are authored in JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) or YAML Ain’t Markup Language (YAML), and include the steps and parameters that you specify.

Next, associate your managed instances with the SSM document. When creating the association, you define the schedule for how often to apply the configured state. Finally, you can choose to write the output of the commands to an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket when you create an association.

Instead of storing sensitive data in configuration files or hard coding them into source code, you can use the Systems Manager Parameter Store to store these parameters, and then reference this information in applications or scripts. Use Parameter Store to store configuration information, such as:
Passwords
Keys
License codes
Database strings

In the example illustrated on the slide, a new parameter was created to store a password. The parameter name is then referenced in the code shown on the right. Parameter Store integrates with IAM to control parameter access, and then the stored information can be encrypted with AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS).

SSM documents currently do not support references to SecureString parameters. This means that to use SecureString parameters with (for example) Run Command, it is necessary to retrieve the parameter value before passing it to Run Command.

notes: The Systems Manager Inventory feature can collect inventory information about EC2 instances and the software installed on them, such as:

The Systems Manager Inventory feature can help provide a comprehensive understanding of the system configurations and installed applications across multiple instances, without the need to log into each instance individually.
The gathered data supports managing application assets, tracking licenses, monitoring file integrity, discovering applications not installed by a traditional installer, and more.

notes: The concept of infrastructure as code is fundamental to cloud computing, and differentiates the cloud from more traditional IT environments. The AWS software development kits (SDKs) and the application programming interfaces (APIs) provide you the tools necessary for applications built on AWS to be managed as 'infrastructure as code.'

AWS provides SDKs that are language-specific. These SDKs also contain APIs for the languages shown on this slide. Both the SDKs and APIs allow a developer to incorporate the connectivity and functionality of the wide range of AWS services into their code without needing to write functions from scratch. The AWS SDKs have extensive documentation on how to use them, including guides on how to get started, developer guides, API references, and community forums or developer blogs.
For more information about the AWS SDKs, see https://aws.amazon.com/getting-started/tools-sdks.

texts: AWS CloudFormation allows a user to create, update, and delete a set of resources spanning multiple AWS services as a single unit (stack).
AWS CloudFormation templates are written in JSON or YAML.
Preview how proposed changes with impact environment
notes: AWS CloudFormation is another useful tool that enables a user to create, update, or delete entire AWS infrastructure deployments predictably and repeatedly.

With AWS CloudFormation, an entire infrastructure can be modeled in a single text file written in JSON or YAML. The text file template can be used to define all the desired AWS resources for a stack. An AWS CloudFormation stack is a collection of AWS resources that can be managed as a single unit. In other words, you can create, update, or delete a collection of resources by creating, updating, or deleting stacks. Resources in the stack can include EC2 instances, Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) instances, virtual private clouds (VPCs), and many other resources created from AWS services.

AWS CloudFormation also allows users to preview how proposed changes to a stack might impact their running resources, such as whether your changes will delete or replace any critical resources. AWS CloudFormation only makes the changes to the stack after the user decides to run them.

Another feature of AWS CloudFormation is drift detection. Performing a drift detection operation on a stack determines whether the stack has drifted from its expected template configuration. If the resource in the stack supports drift detection, the drift detection operation returns detailed information about the drift status of that resource.

notes: AWS CloudFormation supports custom extensions to your stack template that can be built using AWS Lambda. You could write custom provisioning in a Lambda function and configure an AWS CloudFormation stack to trigger the Lambda function when it creates the stack. For example, you could write custom provisioning logic for tasks such as looking up the most recent AMI IDs for use in your stacks.

texts: AWS OpsWorks is a configuration management service.
notes: AWS OpsWorks is another useful tool. It is a configuration management service that provides managed instances of Chef and Puppet. Chef and Puppet are automation platforms that allow you to use code to automate the configurations of your servers. OpsWorks lets you use Chef and Puppet to automate how servers are configured, deployed, and managed across your EC2 instances or on-premises compute environments.
OpsWorks has three offerings: AWS OpsWorks for Chef Automate, AWS OpsWorks for Puppet Enterprise, and AWS OpsWorks Stacks.
For more information about AWS OpsWorks, see https://aws.amazon.com/opsworks/.

notes: Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) provides object storage, and it has many practical uses. One thing it can be used for is to host a static website. By using Amazon S3 for this purpose, the need to deploy a complex or costly runtime infrastructure can be avoided. A static website consists of individual webpages that include static content and optional client-side scripts, but these webpages do not rely on any server-side processing.
Hosting a static website on Amazon S3 involves a few steps:
First, create a bucket in Amazon S3 to store the content of the website.
Then, configure the S3 bucket to enable website hosting and grant public read permission to its content.
Finally, upload the website content to the bucket using the Amazon Management Console or the AWS Command-line Interface (CLI).
Access the website at the endpoint URL that Amazon S3 assigns to it. The endpoint URL includes the bucket name and the name of the Region that contains the bucket, as shown in the diagram.

notes: The endpoint URL assigned to a static website hosted in Amazon S3 conforms to one of the two formats shown in this slide. As previously mentioned, it contains the bucket name and the name of the Region where the bucket was created. The difference between the two formats is that the separator character before the Region name is either a period or a dash depending on the Region that contains the bucket. For example, if the bucket is created in the US West (Oregon) Region, the separator character is a dash; however, if the bucket is created in the EU (Frankfurt) Region, the separator character is a period.

NOTE: Uploaded web content should be stored in an Amazon S3 folder hierarchy that reflects the website content structure. In addition, when enabling a bucket for website hosting, the name of the index document must be provided. This document is the default webpage that Amazon S3 returns when a request is made to the root of the website or one of its subfolders. Make sure that the loaded web content includes this index document at the proper folder level.

notes: Instead of accessing a static website using its Amazon S3 endpoint URL, a user can optionally use the Amazon Route 53 service to map the user’s own domain name to the Amazon S3 endpoint. For example, a user could assign the mompopcafe.com domain name to it, or assign a subdomain name, such as www.mompopcafe.com.

In the example shown in this slide, the root domain, mompopcafe.com, and subdomain, www.mompopcafe.com, are used to access the website. To support this, two buckets are created and configured in Amazon S3, one for each name. One bucket contains the website content, and the other bucket redirects requests to the content bucket. Note that the bucket names must match the domain names that they use. In addition, alias records are created in Amazon Route 53 to map the domain and subdomain names to the corresponding S3 bucket endpoints.

texts: Mom & Pop Café & BakeryCustomer Meeting Preparation
notes: We will now begin to prepare for our customer meeting, where a new problem will be proposed and where we will assist them in finding a solution.
The customer has requested to build a website.

texts: Sophie mentioned to Darsh that she wants a website that will showcase the café visually through images, and provide customers with business details.
Eventually, Sophie would like it to evolve to:
Allow customers to place orders online
Track order history, which could be used to predict supply chain needs
Implement reporting functionality (email delivery of reports)
Handle server outages with high availability and failover
notes: Darsh asked Sophie about the website idea she had mentioned to him earlier. She had told him that she wanted the website to showcase the café visually with images, and also show things like the Café’s contact information, and what menu items the Café offers to customers.
Sophie confirmed her interest in the website. She said she just did not have time to create it herself. She told Darsh that she could see the website eventually evolving so that they could:
Automate inventory based on the orders that customers make through the website
Log client information used for orders
Provide delivery notifications
Predict the increase of sales based on historical trends
Darsh responded that he thought that was a great idea.

texts: Activity 2: Create a static website on Amazon S3
notes: In this activity, you will practice using AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) commands to:
Create an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket.
Create a new AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) user that has full access to the Amazon S3 service.
Upload files to Amazon S3 to host a simple website for the Mom & Pop Café & Bakery.
Create a batch file that can be used to update the static website when you change any of the website files locally.
Once you have completed the activity, clients will be able to access the website you have deployed to Amazon S3 as shown in the diagram on the next slide.

texts: Activity #2 - Amazon S3 hosting topology diagram
notes: In activity 2, the static Mom & Pop Café website is hosted on Amazon S3. After the S3 bucket is created and properly configured for website hosting, a client browser can access the website directly by using the assigned Amazon S3 endpoint URL.
